summary: Clarifies and updates the DANE TLSA specification from RFC 6698 based on implementation experience. It also gives guidance to implementers, operators and protocol developers who want to use DANE records.

eli5.summary: This is a better instruction booklet for a system where a website's name list vouches for its security certificate.

subtitle: Clarifies how to use DANE TLSA records safely: which record types to publish, how to roll keys, and how clients should check them.

tldr.problem: RFC 6698 defined TLSA records, which tie a TLS server's certificate or key to its DNSSEC-signed DNS name. It allows 24 combinations of record fields, and implementation experience showed that many of them are confusing, fragile or hard to roll over.
tldr.mechanism: This document narrows the choices, recommending DANE-EE(3) and DANE-TA(2) with SHA2-256 digests. It adds rules for publishers (keep every parameter combination matching the current certificate chain), for clients (digest algorithm agility, CNAME handling) and for servers (send the trust anchor certificate).
tldr.outcome: It updates RFC 6698 with normative changes and operational advice. It is a Proposed Standard, and no later RFC is listed as obsoleting or updating it.

facts.label: Pre-publish new records
facts.value: At least two TTLs before the change

today: RFC 7671 is a Proposed Standard that updates RFC 6698, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It is meant to be read together with RFC 6698, RFC 7672 and RFC 7673.

sections.title: Why DANE Needed Clarifying
sections.content:
RFC 6698 introduced the DNS TLSA resource record. A TLSA record associates a certificate or a public key, of an end entity or of a trusted issuing authority, with a TLS or DTLS transport endpoint. DANE relies on DNSSEC, and DNSSEC-validated TLSA records can augment or replace the use of trusted public Certification Authorities (CAs).

RFC 6698 defines three fields with four, two and three possible values, which gives 24 combinations. This document recommends a smaller set of best-practice combinations to simplify protocol design, implementation and deployment. It also explains strategies for virtual hosting, where one Service Provider endpoint serves several Customer Domains.

Section 12 of the RFC lists the normative updates it makes to RFC 6698. Related documents are RFC 7673 and RFC 7672.
sections.eli5: The first rulebook for DANE had too many ways to do the same thing, and people got confused. This document picks the best few ways and explains why.

sections.title: The TLSA Record Fields
sections.content:
A TLSA record has four fields. The first three, called the TLSA parameters, say how to read the fourth.

  • Certificate Usage: PKIX-TA(0), PKIX-EE(1), DANE-TA(2) or DANE-EE(3). The value 255 is private use.
  • Selector: Cert(0) for the whole certificate or SPKI(1) for the subject public key. The value 255 is private use.
  • Matching Type: Full(0), SHA2-256(1) or SHA2-512(2). The value 255 is private use.
  • Certificate Association Data: the full value or digest of the certificate or key.

Of the two digest algorithms, only SHA2-256(1) is mandatory to implement. Clients SHOULD implement SHA2-512(2), but servers SHOULD NOT publish only SHA2-512(2) digests.

In the RFC's example, _25._tcp.mail.example.com. IN TLSA 2 0 1 (...) means usage DANE-TA(2), selector Cert(0) and matching type SHA2-256(1), followed by the digest.
sections.eli5: A TLSA record is a label with three small number codes that say what kind of fingerprint follows, and then the fingerprint itself.

sections.title: Choosing Certificate Usages
sections.content:
With PKIX-TA(0) and PKIX-EE(1), both sides need a mutually trusted CA configured in advance. With DANE-TA(2) and DANE-EE(3), the published TLSA records are enough to verify the peer's certificate chain.

Supporting all four usages in a client is NOT RECOMMENDED. An attacker who can break DNSSEC could simply replace the TLSA RRset with DANE-EE(3) or DANE-TA(2) records, so PKIX-TA(0) and PKIX-EE(1) add only illusory extra security. Clients supporting just DANE-TA(2) and DANE-EE(3) are RECOMMENDED.

For DANE-EE(3), the server is authenticated by checking that its leaf certificate matches the record. The server MUST be considered authenticated even if none of the names in the certificate match, and the certificate's expiration date MUST be ignored. The validity of the binding comes from the DNSSEC signatures on the TLSA record.

Most sites are advised to publish DANE-EE(3) SPKI(1) SHA2-256(1) records. SPKI(1) works with raw public keys and survives certificate renewal with the same key, and all implementations must support SHA2-256.

For opportunistic security clients, PKIX-TA(0) and PKIX-EE(1) SHOULD NOT be used, because they are more brittle and no more secure.
sections.eli5: Instead of asking a big list of outside inspectors to vouch for a shop, the shop's own phone book entry says exactly which key to expect. That is simpler and breaks less often.

sections.title: Trust Anchors, CNAMEs and Hosting
sections.content:
For DANE-TA(2), servers MUST include the trust anchor certificate in the TLS certificate message, unless every such TLSA record is a 2 0 0 record that publishes the certificate in full. Clients may ignore locally configured trust anchors for this usage. Server certificates still need names that match the client's reference identifiers, and TLSA records with selector Cert(0) are preferred so that constraints in the trust anchor certificate apply.

For PKIX-TA(0), a client MUST keep extending the chain beyond a locally trusted intermediate, in case a certificate closer to the root matches the TLSA record. PKIX-EE(1) is like DANE-EE(3) but with normal PKIX checks as well.

When a hosting company (the Service Provider) and the TLSA Publisher are the same entity, coordination problems disappear. Only DANE-EE(3) and DANE-TA(2) work well with TLSA CNAMEs across organizations. DANE clients connecting to a name that is a CNAME SHOULD follow it hop by hop, and if every step is DNSSEC "secure" the final target SHOULD be the TLSA base domain, with the original name as a fallback. That name MUST then be used as the SNI HostName.
sections.eli5: If a shop is run by a bigger company, it is easiest if the bigger company keeps the phone book entry too. The document also says to follow a chain of forwarding notes to the real address and check that one.

sections.title: Publishing and Rolling Keys Safely
sections.content:
The TLSA Publisher MUST ensure that each combination of certificate usage, selector and matching type in the RRset includes at least one record that matches the server's current certificate chain. Records for retired or not-yet-deployed chains may exist during a rollover but MUST NOT be the only records for any combination. Clients support different subsets of parameters, so each combination must be sufficient on its own.

For a key rollover with fixed parameters, the safe sequence is:

  1. Add records matching the future key at least two TTLs before the new chain is deployed.
  2. Deploy the new chain and check that it works.
  3. Remove the records for the old chain.

When adding a new parameter combination, publish it first for the existing chain and only then deploy new keys. When adding a digest algorithm, publish it for every usage and selector pair and key that already has another digest. The RFC's summary advice is to make one change at a time.
sections.eli5: When you change the lock on a door, you first tell everyone about the new key, wait until the news has spread, and only then swap the lock. Never remove the old key until the new one is already working.

sections.title: Digest Algorithm Agility and Record Size
sections.content:
RFC 6698 had no way for a client to prefer the strongest shared digest. Here, clients SHOULD keep a configurable order of digest algorithms by strength. After discarding unusable or malformed records, for each usage and selector the client SHOULD process only the Full(0) records and the usable records with the strongest digest algorithm.

In the RFC's example, a client preferring SHA2-512(2) over SHA2-256(1) sees 3 1 1, 3 1 2 and 3 1 0 records. It SHOULD accept a key matching the 3 1 0 or 3 1 2 record, but SHOULD NOT accept a key matching only the weaker 3 1 1 record.

Deployments SHOULD avoid TLSA record sizes that cause UDP fragmentation. Matching type Full(0) is NOT RECOMMENDED, and publishing both Cert(0) and Full(0) SHOULD NOT be done, since a single certificate is generally too large to deliver reliably over UDP. A digest such as SHA2-256(1) SHOULD be used, with the complete certificate sent in the TLS handshake.
sections.eli5: If a shop lists a weak fingerprint and a strong one, you should trust the strong one when you can read it. Also, keep the entry short so it fits in one envelope.

sections.title: DNSSEC Dependence and Security Notes
sections.content:
The security of DANE rests on DNSSEC. Only the registrar of record can update a domain's DS record in the parent zone, so DNS operators are advised to set a registrar lock against unauthorized domain transfers. TLSA Publishers are advised to pick a registrar that lets domains move without disabling DNSSEC.

DNSSEC-signed RRsets cannot be securely revoked before they expire. For high-value keys, a signature lifetime of a few days is reasonable, with daily re-signing. For less critical data, a couple of weeks to a month is reasonable, with weekly re-signing. If a zone is not re-signed in time, the whole domain becomes "bogus", so monitoring is important.

TLSA TTLs need care: clients that cache stale records will fail after an unplanned change. If TLSA records are all unusable, a client in mandatory-authentication mode MUST NOT connect. An opportunistic client SHOULD connect with unauthenticated TLS and MUST NOT connect if TLS cannot be established. DANE-EE(3) and DANE-TA(2) clients also SHOULD NOT perform Certificate Transparency checks.
sections.eli5: The phone book is only as trustworthy as its seal. Keep the seal fresh, watch that it does not run out, and do not use a stale entry if a key gets stolen.

items.label: PKIX-TA
items.desc: Constrains which PKIX CAs may issue; not recommended when the provider is not also the publisher.

items.label: PKIX-EE
items.desc: Like DANE-EE but PKIX checks (names, expiry, CT) still apply.

items.label: DANE-TA
items.desc: Publishes a trust anchor; server must send the TA certificate in its chain.

items.label: DANE-EE
items.desc: Matches the server leaf certificate or key; name checks and expiry are ignored.

data.title: Rollover with fixed parameters
data.code:
; Initial
_443._tcp.www.example.org. IN TLSA 3 1 1 01d09d19c2139a46...

; Transitional, at least two TTLs before the key change
_443._tcp.www.example.org. IN TLSA 3 1 1 01d09d19c2139a46...
_443._tcp.www.example.org. IN TLSA 3 1 1 7aa7a5359173d05b...

; Final, after the key change
_443._tcp.www.example.org. IN TLSA 3 1 1 7aa7a5359173d05b...
